title: The magi, the demons, and the star
source_text: Πρὸς μὲν οὖν Ἕλληνας, ὅτι μάγοι δαίμοσιν ὁμιλοῦντες καὶ τούτους ἐφ᾿ ἃ μεμαθήκασι καὶ βούλονται καλοῦντες ποιοῦσι μὲν τὸ τοιοῦτον, ὅσον οὐδὲν θειότερον καὶ ἰσχυρότερον τῶν δαιμόνων καὶ τῆς καλούσης αὐτοὺς ἐπῳδῆς ἐπιφαίνεται ἢ λέγεται· ἐὰν δὲ θειοτέρα τις ἐπιφάνεια γένηται, καθαιροῦνται αἱ τῶν δαιμόνων ἐνέργειαι, μὴ δυνάμεναι ἀντιβλέψαι τῷ τῆς θειότητος φωτί. εἰκὸς οὖν καὶ κατὰ τὴν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ γένεσιν, ἐπεὶ „πλῆθος στρατιᾶς οὐρανίου,“ ὡς ὁ Λουκᾶς ἀνέγραψε κἀγὼ πείθομαι, ᾔνεσε τὸν θεὸν καὶ ἔλεγε· „δόξα ἐν ὑψίστοις θεῷ καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς εἰρήνη, ἐν ἀνθρώποις εὐδοκία,“ διὰ τοῦτο οἱ δαίμονες ἠτόνησαν καὶ ἐξησθένησαν, ἐλεγχθείσης αὐτῶν τῆς γοητείας καὶ καταλυθείσης τῆς ἐνεργείας, οὐ μόνον ὑπὸ τῶν ἐπιδημησάντων τῷ περιγείῳ τόπῳ ἀγγέλων διὰ τὴν Ἰησοῦ γένεσιν καθαιρεθέντες ἀλλὰ καὶ ὑπὸ τῆς ψυχῆς τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ τῆς ἐν αὐτῷ θειότητος. οἱ τοίνυν μάγοι τὰ συνήθη πράττειν θέλοντες, ἅπερ πρότερον διά τινων ἐπῳδῶν καὶ μαγγανειῶν ἐποίουν, ἐζήτησαν τὴν αἰτίαν, μεγάλην αὐτὴν εἶναι τεκμαιρόμενοι, καὶ ἰδόντες θεοσημίαν ἐν οὐρανῷ ἐβούλοντο τὸ σημαινόμενον ἀπ᾿ αὐτῆς ἰδεῖν. δοκεῖ μοι οὖν ὅτι ἔχοντες τοῦ Βαλαὰμ ἃς καὶ Μω(??)σῆς ἀνέγραψε προφητείας, ὡς καὶ αὐτοῦ περὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα γενομένου δεινοῦ, καὶ εὑρόντες ἐκεῖ περὶ τοῦ ἄστρου καὶ τὸ „δείξω αὐτῷ. καὶ οὐχὶ νῦν· μακαρίζω, καὶ οὐκ ἐγγιεῖ“ ἐστοχάσαντο τὸν μετὰ τοῦ ἄστρου προφητεύομενον ἄνθρωπον ἐπιδεδημηκέναι τῷ βίῳ, καὶ ὡς πάντων δαιμόνων καὶ τῶν ἐν ἔθει αὐτοῖς φανταζομένων καὶ ἐνεργούντων κρείττονα προλαβόντες „προσκυνῆσαι“ ἠθέλησαν. ἧκον οὖν ἐπὶ τὴν Ἰουδαίαν, ὅτι μὲν „βασιλεύς“ τις γεγέννηται πειθόμενοι ἢ ποῦ γεννηθήσεται γινώσκοντες, τίνα δὲ βασιλείαν βασιλεύσων οὐκ ἐπιστάμενοι· φέροντες μὲν „δῶρα“, (ἃ) , ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, συνθέτῳ τινὶ ἐκ θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπου θνητοῦ „προσήνεγκαν“, σύμβολα μὲν ὡς βασιλεῖ τὸν „χρυσὸν“ ὡς δὲ τεθνηξομένῳ τὴν „σμύρναν“, ὡς δὲ θεῷ τὸν λιβανωτόν· „προσήνεγκαν“ δὲ μαθόντες τὸν τόπον τῆς γενέσεως αὐτοῦ. ἀλλ᾿ ἐπεὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ ὑπὲρ τοὺς βοηθοῦντας ἀνθρώποις ἀγγέλους ἐνυπάρχων σωτὴρ τοῦ γένους τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ἄγγελος ἠμείψατο τὴν τῶν μάγων ἐπὶ τὸ προσκυνῆσαι τὸν Ἰησοῦν εὐσέβειαν, χρηματίσας αὐτοῖς μὴ ἥκειν πρὸς τὸν Ἡρώδην ἀλλ᾿ ἐπανελθεῖν ἄλλῃ ὁδῷ εἰς τὰ οἰκεῖα.
pass_a_gloss: To (πρός) the Greeks, then: that magi (μάγοι), consorting (ὁμιλοῦντες) with demons (δαίμοσιν) and calling (καλοῦντες) them for what they have learned (μεμαθήκασι) and wish, do such a thing so long as nothing more divine (θειότερον) and stronger than the demons and the incantation (ἐπῳδή) calling them appears (ἐπιφαίνεται) or is spoken; but if some more divine manifestation (ἐπιφάνεια) happens, the operations (ἐνέργειαι) of the demons are pulled down (καθαιροῦνται), not able to look against (ἀντιβλέψαι) the light of the divinity (θειότης). Likely (εἰκός) then also at the birth (γένεσις) of Jesus, since 'a multitude of heavenly host (στρατιᾶς οὐρανίου)', as Luke recorded and I am persuaded, praised (ᾔνεσε) God and said 'glory in highest to God and on earth peace, among men good pleasure (εὐδοκία)', for this the demons slackened (ἠτόνησαν) and became weak (ἐξησθένησαν), their sorcery (γοητεία) refuted (ἐλεγχθείσης) and their operation dissolved (καταλυθείσης), pulled down not only by the angels who sojourned (ἐπιδημησάντων) in the region around the earth (περιγείῳ τόπῳ) because of Jesus' birth but also by the soul (ψυχή) of Jesus and the divinity in him. So the magi, wishing to do the customary things, which formerly they did through certain incantations and trickeries (μαγγανειῶν), sought the cause, judging (τεκμαιρόμενοι) it great, and seeing a divine sign (θεοσημίαν) in heaven wished to see what was signified by it. It seems to me then that having the prophecies of Balaam which Moses too recorded, as he himself too had been clever (δεινοῦ) about such things, and finding there about the star (ἄστρον) and 'I will show him, and not now; I bless/call blessed (μακαρίζω), and he does not draw near (ἐγγιεῖ)', they conjectured (ἐστοχάσαντο) that the man prophesied with the star had arrived in life (ἐπιδεδημηκέναι τῷ βίῳ), and having assumed beforehand (προλαβόντες) [him] stronger (κρείττονα) than all demons and those habitually appearing to them and working, wished to 'worship (προσκυνῆσαι)'. They came then to Judea, persuaded that a 'king' had been born or knowing where he will be born, but not knowing what kingdom he would reign; bringing 'gifts', which, that I may so name it, to a certain compound (συνθέτῳ) of God and mortal man they 'offered', symbols (σύμβολα): as to a king the 'gold', as to one about to die (τεθνηξομένῳ) the 'myrrh', as to God the frankincense; and they 'offered' having learned the place of his birth. But since the Saviour (σωτήρ) of the human race, existing above the angels who help men, was God (θεός), an angel repaid (ἠμείψατο) the piety (εὐσέβεια) of the magi toward worshipping Jesus, warning (χρηματίσας) them not to come to Herod but to go back by another road to their own [land].
pass_b_english: To the Greeks, then, we would say this. Magi, who have dealings with demons and summon them for the purposes they have learned and desire, achieve such things only so long as nothing more divine and more powerful than the demons and the incantation that summons them appears or is spoken. But if some more divine manifestation takes place, the workings of the demons are overthrown, since they cannot face the light of the Godhead. It is likely, then, that at the birth of Jesus too, since “a multitude of the heavenly host,” as Luke recorded and as I believe, praised God and said, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill among men” (Luke 2:13–14), the demons for this reason lost their strength and grew weak. Their sorcery was exposed and their working undone; they were overthrown not only by the angels who visited the region around the earth because of the birth of Jesus, but also by the soul of Jesus and the Godhead in him.

So the magi, wishing to do what they were used to doing, which they had formerly done by certain incantations and tricks, looked for the cause, judging that it must be a great one; and seeing a sign from God in the sky, they wanted to see what it signified. It seems to me, then, that they had the prophecies of Balaam, which Moses also recorded, since Balaam himself had been skilled in such arts. There they found what is said about the star, and the words, “I will show him, but not now; I call him blessed, but he will not draw near” (Numbers 24:17). From this they guessed that the man foretold together with the star had come into the world; and having concluded beforehand that he was stronger than all the demons and than the beings that usually appeared to them and worked for them, they wished “to worship” him (Matthew 2:2).

They came, then, to Judea, convinced that some “king” had been born (Matthew 2:2), or knowing where he would be born, but not understanding over what kind of kingdom he would reign. They brought “gifts,” and these they “offered” to one who was, if I may call him so, a kind of compound of God and mortal man: gold as a symbol for a king, myrrh as for one who would die, and frankincense as for God (Matthew 2:11). And they “offered” them after they had learned the place of his birth (Matthew 2:9–11). But since the Saviour of the human race, who exists above the angels who help human beings, was God, an angel repaid the magi for their reverence in worshipping Jesus: he warned them not to go to Herod but to return to their own country by another way (Matthew 2:12).

choices.choice: The chapter carries out the plan announced at the end of 1.59 (some things to be said to the Greeks, others to the Jews); 'we would say this' supplies the verb implied from 1.59 (τοιαῦτα ἂν εἴποιμεν). The staged text has Μω(??)σῆς; read Μωϋσῆς (Moses). Koetschau supplies (ἃ) before ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω; followed. Numbers 24:17 is quoted from the Septuagint (δείξω αὐτῷ καὶ οὐχὶ νῦν· μακαρίζω καὶ οὐκ ἐγγίζει; Origen's text has the future ἐγγιεῖ, rendered as a future, 'he will not draw near'); the LXX wording differs from the Hebrew ('I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near'). The phrase ἢ ποῦ γεννηθήσεται γινώσκοντες ('or knowing where he would be born') sits oddly between the μέν and δέ clauses and may be corrupt; it is translated as it stands. Matthew 2:4-6 (the chief priests telling Herod where the Christ was to be born) is listed in bible_refs as probable background only and is not cited inline, because in Matthew the magi themselves do not know the place. 'Gifts', 'offered', 'king' and 'to worship' are Matthew's words (Matthew 2:2, 2:11); Origen quotes them as single words. The order gold, myrrh, frankincense is Origen's. θειότης is rendered 'Godhead' where it means the divinity of God or of Christ. 'The Saviour ... was God' renders θεὸς ἦν with θεός as predicate.
ἀντιβλέψαι: 'cannot look back at' (reads as looking backward) changed to 'cannot face'
ἐπιδημησάντων: 'came down to' changed to 'visited' (no descent in the Greek)
Numbers 24:17: future ἐγγιεῖ kept as future, 'he will not draw near'; note updated
removed inline (Matthew 2:4–6) after 'knowing where he would be born': in Matthew the magi do not know the place, so the verse does not say this; kept in bible_refs as background
checked Luke 2:13–14, Matthew 2:2, 2:9–12 against the clauses they sit beside
